analysis.title: Global Memory & Storage: HBF Deep Dive - Could HBF be the solution to the Memory bottleneck?
key_insights: Bernstein argues AI is shifting from compute-centric to memory-centric as inference and agentic workloads grow. Larger models and longer context push data beyond HBM into DRAM, NAND and HDD, broadening memory demand.

Epoch AI estimates frontier LLM training compute has grown about 5x per year since 2020, while GPU memory bandwidth has grown about 28% per year since 2008. Bernstein cites this as the widening memory wall.
LLM inference decoding is often memory-bandwidth-bound, and MoE models cut compute per token without cutting memory needs because the full parameter set must stay accessible.
AI labs and Google price cached-token reads at about 10% of fresh input tokens. This gives an economic incentive to store and reuse KV cache instead of recomputing it.
HBF (high-bandwidth flash) targets HBM-class read bandwidth with 8-16x HBM capacity. Bernstein expects an HBF stack could be priced near an HBM stack, which implies a much lower cost per GB.

In a tiered design, HBM keeps the active working set while HBF holds inactive MoE experts, model weights and warm or reusable KV cache. SK hynix's H3 architecture proposes a similar HBM plus HBF hierarchy.

Sandisk's internal simulation on Qwen3-480B-A35B (960GB bfloat16) showed one HBF GPU could host the model versus a minimum of eight HBM GPUs. It also showed four HBF GPUs matching the token output of eight HBM GPUs. Bernstein notes these are internal simulations, not third-party benchmarks.

Most emerging new-tier technologies are NAND-based (HBF, Storage Next SLC SSDs, Z-NAND, XL-FLASH, NVIDIA CMX), except CXL-attached DRAM. Bernstein says their adoption should consume NAND wafer supply and tighten NAND supply/demand regardless of which architecture wins.

Bernstein estimates an HBF-to-NAND wafer trade ratio of 6.5x in the base case (4.3x low, 8.7x high), versus about 3x for HBM-to-DRAM. The build is 2.9x TLC-to-SLC density penalty x 1.725x die-area penalty x 1.3x yield penalty.

Illustrative sensitivity: if 10-20% of TLC-equivalent GB demand moved to higher-performance NAND at a 3-7x trade ratio, industry wafer needs would rise about 20-120%. Bernstein says this is not its official demand forecast.

Bernstein estimates HBF cost at roughly 10x enterprise SSD cost per GB (base 11.5x for 8-hi, 9.5x for 16-hi). Module cost is about $164 for an 8-hi 256GB stack and $271 for a 16-hi 512GB stack in the base case.
At a base-case HBF ASP of $4.75/GB (HBM4 at $38/GB for 2027), Bernstein estimates gross margin of about 88.9% for 16-hi and 86.5% for 8-hi HBF. That compares with Sandisk's 84.6% FQ4 gross margin.
Bernstein cautions HBF pricing depends on HBM pricing and the DRAM/NAND cycle. Micron said HBM margin will stay below conventional DRAM margin in 2027, and a similar dynamic could apply to HBF.
Bernstein sees HBF as more likely to complement than replace HBM. It also sees a Jevons Paradox in which cheaper inference raises aggregate HBM and GPU demand.

Architectural limits of HBF: microsecond NAND read latency versus nanoseconds for DRAM, page-level reads that waste bandwidth on scattered access, and slow writes with finite endurance. Because HBF sits inside a CoWoS package, a worn-out HBF means replacing the whole accelerator.

Biggest adoption concern: NVIDIA has not endorsed HBF and instead promotes CMX and Storage Next. KIOXIA also highlights CMX and Storage Next, TSMC has not mentioned preparation, and none of NVIDIA's Rubin, Rubin Ultra or Feynman (volume 2028) feature HBF. Bernstein says any NVIDIA adoption is a few years out.

HBF consortium members are Sandisk, Google, SK hynix, Tenstorrent and Meta (added August 2026). The first spec was released in August 2026. Sandisk has taped out its first HBF die and targets first inference-product samples in 2027. HBF is outside Sandisk's published financial targets, so it is potential upside.

risk_factors: NVIDIA has not officially endorsed HBF and promotes CMX and Storage Next. Bernstein says any NVIDIA adoption is a few years out.
KIOXIA has not announced HBF support and highlights CMX and Storage Next instead, and TSMC has not mentioned preparation.
HBF needs processor and software redesign, and pairing it with GPUs used for both training and inference makes them effective only for inference.
CoWoS package space is scarce and its allocation to HBF over compute or HBM is debatable.
HBF inherits NAND's latency, page-level read, write speed and endurance limits, and a failed HBF requires replacing the accelerator.
HBF profitability depends on HBM pricing, the DRAM/NAND cycle and the economics of AI.
HBF could reduce HBM and GPU content per workload, though Bernstein expects Jevons Paradox to offset that.
SLC use in HBF has not been officially confirmed.
charts_described: Exhibit 5 shows cache-read pricing at 10% of input for most models (OpenAI gpt-5.6 family, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash), 50% for gpt-4o, and about 0.8% for DeepSeek V4-Pro and about 2% for V4-Flash.
Exhibit 3 shows the memory hierarchy with approximate prices: SRAM $3,000/GB, HBM $20/GB, DRAM $25/GB, enterprise SSD $0.30/GB, HDD $0.016/GB, tape $0.008/GB.
Exhibit 19 compares HBM (about 2-3.3 TB/s for HBM4, fast cells around 100 ns) with HBF (0.4-3 TB/s target, slow cells in microseconds).
Exhibit 20 shows approximate read latency: SLC single-digit to 25 microseconds, MLC 30-50, TLC 60-100, QLC 120-200.

tension_points.bull_case: HBF could do for NAND what HBM did for DRAM: 6.5x wafer trade ratio, gross margins of 80-90%, and new AI demand. Other NAND-based tiers (Storage Next, CMX, Z-NAND) could tighten NAND supply even if HBF stalls.
tension_points.bear_case: NVIDIA, KIOXIA and TSMC have not endorsed or prepared for HBF. NVIDIA's roadmap through Feynman in 2028 has no HBF, and HBF has latency, endurance, serviceability and CoWoS-space limits.
tension_points.what_invalidates: NVIDIA continuing to exclude HBF from its roadmap, which Bernstein says would put any adoption a few years out.

tension_points.theme: HBF effect on HBM and GPU demand
tension_points.bull_case: Jevons Paradox: cheaper inference could drive more total HBM and GPU demand, and HBF complements HBM.
tension_points.bear_case: HBF could reduce HBM and GPU content per workload, with Sandisk's simulation showing one HBF GPU replacing eight HBM GPUs for capacity.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Higher GPU intensity per workload being outweighed by deployment growth is the swing factor. The report names no price or date threshold.

theme_stances.key_argument: HBF could create new premium AI demand and consume far more wafer capacity per bit, tightening NAND supply and supporting pricing and margins.
theme_stances.evidence: HBF could do for NAND what HBM did for DRAM industry dynamics.
